opus-5.5.text:
I think the timing is right because several things have come together at once. A few years ago the models simply weren't capable enough. You could ask them to help with research, but most of what came back was surface-level: they could summarize papers, but they couldn't reason through a problem, write nontrivial code that actually ran, or tell when an experimental result didn't make sense. That has changed quite dramatically. The models can now carry out fairly long chains of reasoning, write and debug code, run experiments, and iterate on the results. Once a model can close that loop, even partially, AI-driven research becomes a real question rather than science fiction.

The second factor is that the traditional scaling path is starting to show its limits. We've used up much of the high-quality human data, and simply making models bigger brings diminishing returns relative to cost. So the field has to ask where the next gains come from. One very natural answer is to have the models generate new knowledge themselves: proposing hypotheses, verifying them, and feeding what they learn back into training. That's essentially what recursive self-improvement means in practice. It isn't a sudden "intelligence explosion." It's a steady loop in which the system helps improve the next version of itself.

The third factor is something I care about personally: understanding. For a long time we've treated these models largely as black boxes. We train them, they work, and we don't fully know why. If AI is going to do research, including research on AI, we need a much deeper understanding of the learning dynamics: how representations form, why certain features emerge, what the optimization is really doing. Without that, self-improvement is just blind trial and error at very large scale. With it, the process becomes far more efficient, and frankly safer, because you know what you're steering.

Finally, there's the human side. Many researchers, myself included, spend a huge share of their time on mechanical work: tuning, rerunning experiments, writing boilerplate. If AI can take over that part, humans can focus on asking the right questions and making judgment calls about what's worth pursuing. I see this less as AI replacing researchers and more as changing what a researcher's job is. Taste, insight, and knowing which problem matters become even more important.

So it's a combination of capability reaching a threshold, the old paradigm running out of room, and a real scientific opportunity to understand these systems more deeply. That's why I think now is the moment to push in this direction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few things coming together right now. The first is that the models have crossed a threshold where they can actually do meaningful pieces of the research loop themselves. A year or two ago, you could ask a model to summarize a paper or write some boilerplate, but it couldn't really propose a hypothesis, implement it, run the experiment, look at the result, and decide what to try next. Now that whole cycle is starting to work, at least for narrow, well-defined problems. And once that cycle closes, even imperfectly, you get compounding returns, because the thing that is doing the research is also the thing being improved.

The second reason is that the bottleneck in AI research has shifted. It used to be compute and data. Those still matter, but increasingly the bottleneck is human attention. There are far more promising ideas than there are researchers to try them. If you look at a typical lab, most of the day is spent on infrastructure, debugging, ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, writing up results. Very little of it is the creative leap. If models can absorb the mechanical part, a single researcher can explore ten or a hundred times more of the idea space. That is a very different regime.

The third thing, and this is more of a personal reason, is that I have spent a long time thinking about search and self-play, going back to the Go work and planning. Recursive self-improvement is really the same structure. You have a system that generates candidates, evaluates them, and uses the evaluation to generate better candidates. The difference is that now the search space is research ideas and code rather than board positions. The tools to study that rigorously, to measure whether the loop is actually improving versus just producing noise, are finally available. So it feels like the right moment to treat this as a science rather than a slogan.

I do want to be careful about the term, though. Recursive self-improvement sounds dramatic, but in practice what we are seeing is more like incremental acceleration. The model helps you find a better optimizer, which helps you train a slightly better model, which is a slightly better research assistant. Nobody has shown an unbounded takeoff, and I am skeptical that it works that way. But even modest compounding changes how fast the field moves, and I would rather be studying it carefully now than reacting to it later.

astra-6.text:
I think the key change is that AI is becoming useful in the research process itself. It can help write code, run experiments, analyze results, and suggest what to try next. That gives us an opportunity to move from an AI that answers questions to an AI that participates in a cycle of discovery.

Research requires a lot of iteration. You have an idea, test it, discover that something is wrong, and revise it. If AI can help shorten that loop, even without coming up with a major breakthrough on its own, it can accelerate progress. And when the subject of that research is AI, you get the possibility of a feedback loop: better models help us do better research, which helps us build better models.

But I would distinguish that possibility from saying recursive self-improvement is already solved. Generating ideas or producing code is only part of the problem. You need reliable experiments and evaluations that tell you whether a change actually makes things better. Otherwise, you can automate a lot of activity without making progress.

So I see this as a good time to work on the problem because we can start testing these loops concretely. We can give a system a bounded research task, measure the outcome, and understand where human judgment is still needed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that AI is starting to help with the process of research itself, not just with a specific task at the end. It can help write code, explore ideas, design experiments, and analyze results. That creates an opportunity to build a feedback loop: use AI to improve how we do research, then use that research to build better AI.

Of course, a feedback loop doesn’t automatically mean recursive self-improvement. The difficult part is knowing whether a proposed change is actually better. You need reliable evaluations, reproducible experiments, and a way to distinguish a real advance from something that just looks promising.

That’s why I see this as a good time to pursue it. We can start with bounded problems where progress is measurable, study where the loop works and where it breaks, and gradually give the system more responsibility. The interesting question is how much of the research cycle we can make genuinely productive and reliable.
